authoredPrompt: This figure sets four triangle sketches in a row, labeled (a) through (d) below, to enumerate the possible outcomes when two sides and a non-included angle are known. All four share one labeling scheme: an acute angle alpha marked by an arc at the left end of a horizontal base, a vertex beta at the right end of that base, an apex gamma above, side b rising from alpha to gamma, and side a hanging from gamma. Panel (a), headed No triangle, a < h, draws a as a short vertical segment from gamma that stops above the base, leaving a visible gap so nothing closes. Panel (b), headed Right triangle, a = h, has a reaching the base exactly at beta, with a small square marking the right angle formed there. Panel (c), headed Two triangles, a > h, a < b, shows a solid vertical altitude labeled h from gamma to the base, plus two dashed segments each labeled a running from gamma to different landing points, one to the left of the altitude's foot and one at beta. Panel (d), headed One triangle, a is greater than or equal to b, shows a broad triangle whose side a slopes from gamma down to beta. Aligning the four under identical labels isolates the one quantity that changes, the length of a measured against the altitude and against b, and shows how many closures each case admits.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for side length a: the learner drags the candidate side a while alpha and b stay fixed, the construction passes through no triangle, right triangle, two triangles, and one triangle, showing that the number of possible closures depends on comparing a with h and b.
- Toggle for showing altitude h: the learner turns the altitude guide on or off, the threshold line and right-angle marker appear across the panels, making clear why a below h cannot reach the base and a equal to h gives exactly one right triangle.
- Button/state for case stepping: the learner advances through the four named cases one at a time, the active panel highlights its closing side or gap, connecting each inequality for a to the visible geometric outcome.
authoredContext:
Oblique triangles in the category SSA may have four different outcomes. The figure illustrates the solutions with the known sides a and b and known angle α.

Four attempted oblique triangles are in a row, all with standard labels. Side c is the horizontal base. In the first attempted triangle, side a is less than the altitude height. Since side a cannot reach side c, there is no triangle. In the second attempted triangle, side a is equal to the length of the altitude height, so side a forms a right angle with side c. In the third attempted triangle, side a is greater than the altitude height and less than side b, so side a can form either an acute or obtuse angle with side c. In the fourth attempted triangle, side a is greater than or equal to side b, so side a forms an acute angle with side c.

discrepancies: Source uses uniform thin black strokes throughout; the generated figure colors side a red and the alternate triangle blue-dashed, which deviates from the monochrome textbook look (though it aids the interaction)

In case (c) the source shows both candidate sides a as identical dashed lines symmetric about h; the generated version draws one solid red and one blue dashed, implying an asymmetry between the two solutions

The four cases are shown one at a time behind a Next-case button rather than simultaneously as four panels — acceptable as a toggle, but the at-a-glance comparison of all four cases in the source is lost by default

In case (a) the source draws side a as a plain segment ending above the base; the generated version adds a red endpoint dot and a dashed altitude h in the same view, slightly cluttering the 'no triangle' case
evaluation.notes: The single-panel interactive replacement faithfully reproduces all four SSA cases with correct geometry (altitude h = b·sinα, right-angle case, two-solution case, obtuse single case) and a well-designed slider + case-stepper, though the red/blue coloring departs from the source's monochrome style and case (c) visually privileges one solution over the other.

Add a small persistent indicator of which of the four cases (a)–(d) is active, e.g. four clickable case tabs, to recover the source's at-a-glance four-panel comparison
